title: the Brahmanda
hook: the gods are losing, so they build a fire, and a goddess rises out of it
tomorrow: a hymn with no story, only names. why would that work?

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Brahmanda, the Purana named for Brahma's egg, every world inside one shell. Today, a story tradition places inside that same Purana, and it starts in a fire.

It's the moment in every group project when someone types: okay, nothing is working. The gods are there. A demon named Bhanda has taken their worlds, and every plan has failed. So they build a fire for a great sacrifice and start offering into it, and in the telling, when there's nothing left to give, they offer themselves. The flames climb. Something climbs with them: a goddess, young and shining. And what she's holding is not what anyone expects a warrior to hold.
screen: `NOTHING IS WORKING.` → `THE GODS OFFER EVERYTHING.` → `A GODDESS RISES FROM THE FIRE.`

segments.voice: She is Lalita, and this is the Lalitopakhyana, the account of Lalita. Hayagriva, the horse-headed form of Vishnu, tells it to the sage Agastya. In her hands: a noose, an elephant goad, a bow made of sugarcane, and arrows made of flowers. To see why, look at the enemy. In the telling, Bhanda is born from ashes, the ashes of Kama, the god of desire, after Shiva burns him with the fire of his third eye. So the demon is desire that was burned but not gone, desire gone sour. And the goddess rides out armed with sweetness and blossoms, the very things desire reaches for. With an army of goddesses behind her, she meets Bhanda, and he falls. Then the surprise. After the battle, at the gods' asking, Kama is given back his life. The story doesn't end with desire wiped out. It ends with desire returned to the world, in the goddess's hand. Something to tell a friend tonight: the goddess who defeats desire gone wrong fights with a bow made of sugarcane. Devotees in the Shri Vidya tradition worship Lalita as the great goddess, and some readers hear the battle as one fought inside a person.
screen: `A SUGARCANE BOW, FLOWER ARROWS.` · `BHANDA, FROM DESIRE'S ASHES.` · `THE GODDESS RIDES OUT.` · then, large: `DESIRE GIVEN BACK ITS LIFE.`

segments.voice: If a candle or lamp is near, let your eyes rest on its flame; if not, any small light will do. Keep looking for the whole sit. When a want comes up, don't push it away and don't chase it: set it beside the light, and go back to looking. If you pray, you can offer it there.
The Brahmanda: the Purana named for Brahma's egg, and the home tradition gives Lalita's story.
Your line: the Brahmanda. A goddess out of the fire, with flowers for arrows. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Devotees of the goddess Lalita, especially in the Shri Vidya tradition, read and retell the Lalitopakhyana, and her hymn of names, which tradition places in the same Purana, is recited in homes and temples.

Lalita.meaning: the goddess who rises from the gods' sacrificial fire

Bhanda.meaning: the demon born from the ashes of Kama

Hayagriva.meaning: the horse-headed form of Vishnu, who tells the story

Agastya.meaning: the sage who hears Lalita's story

Kama.meaning: the god of desire, burned by Shiva's third eye
